title: Fortune's wheel
hookLine: Lady Philosophy: Fortune turns her wheel, and you knew she was fickle (Consolation 2)

lines: CHAMPIONS ONE YEAR, LAST THE NEXT.
A WHEEL, A CROWN, A FALL.
cards: Your team wins the championship one year and finishes last the next. A stock soars, then sinks. A friend's business is on the news in spring and closed by fall.
Up, then down, and the down tends to land as something personal. Medieval artists drew it as a great wheel: a crowned figure at the top, someone falling off the side, someone crushed at the bottom.
One book gave that wheel a voice, the book from yesterday. Today: Fortune's wheel.

teach.b: First, the diagnosis. In book two of the Consolation, Philosophy tells Boethius he isn't suffering because Fortune changed. He's suffering because he forgot what she is.
You knew her, she says. Her only constancy is change. If she stopped turning, she wouldn't be Fortune.

teach.h: FORTUNE SPEAKS: IT WAS ALL LENT.
teach.b: Second, Fortune speaks. Philosophy lets her talk for herself, and Fortune says, in effect: everything you had, wealth, honors, family glory, was mine, lent to you. I turn my wheel; that's my game.
I bring the low up and the high down. Climb on if you like, but don't call it unjust when the turn brings you down. Third, the comfort that isn't fake.
Philosophy doesn't say the loss doesn't hurt.
She reminds Boethius what Fortune never took: people who love him, his wife and sons still living, and his own mind, which no turn of the wheel can reach.
And she adds something sharp: bad fortune can teach more than good. Good fortune flatters; bad fortune shows you your real friends. Fourth, a neighbor's version.
The Stoic Epictetus said much the same in plainer words: never say of anything, I have lost it; say, I have given it back.
Boethius gave the idea a picture people could hold: a turning wheel, and a voice explaining it.

how: Readers of Boethius use the image of Fortune's wheel to meet gains and losses with less surprise, turning their attention to what no turn of fortune can take.

o: Fortune turning, lifting people up and dropping them
a game of chance played at a medieval fair
a lucky streak that always comes back around

p: all you had was lent to you
shows who your real friends are

s: Philosophy tells Boethius his loss doesn't really hurt
she doesn't deny the pain; she reminds him what the wheel never took.
in book two, Fortune herself speaks
Philosophy lets her say that everything was lent, and turning is her game.
Philosophy says bad fortune can teach more than good
good fortune flatters; bad fortune reveals true friends.

games.q: you're Boethius, and you've just lost everything. Philosophy asks why you're so shocked. what's her answer?
o: you forgot what Fortune is: she always turns.
you'll get it all back soon.
games.why: Philosophy's diagnosis: Boethius knew Fortune's nature and forgot it. if she stopped turning, she wouldn't be Fortune.

practice: Picture a slow wheel turning, and think of one recent turn of it in your life, up or down, something given or something taken. Then ask what the wheel didn't touch: who's still with you, and what's still yours inside.
Rest there, at the hub, where the turning is slowest.

wordCard.voice: Fortune's wheel. In the Consolation, Fortune turns her wheel, lifting and dropping, and Philosophy says: you always knew she was like this. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the wheel of Fortune. The wheel Boethius's Fortune turns in book two.

carryVoice: Your line: the wheel turns. The hub stays where it is. Day six hundred fifty-nine, done.
